title: Destructuring Arrays and Objects
objective: Pull values out of an array or object into named variables in a single line.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Original Code Forge lesson covering a modern JS feature not broken out as its own book section. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Destructuring lets you unpack values from an array or object straight into named variables, instead of reading each one out by hand. const [first, second] = ["Ada", "Bram"] creates first and second in one line, matched by position.

Object destructuring works by property name instead of position: const { name, rank } = apprentice creates variables named name and rank, pulled from the matching properties on apprentice — the variable names must match the property names.

You can skip array elements you don't need with an empty slot (const [, second] = arr skips the first), and give an object-destructured variable a different local name with const { name: apprenticeName } = apprentice.
explanation.rule: Array destructuring matches by position: const [a, b] = arr. Object destructuring matches by property name: const { key } = obj.

examples.title: Destructuring an Array
examples.note: x and y are created in one line, matched to point's elements by position.

examples.title: Destructuring an Object
examples.note: name and rank are pulled out by matching property name, not position — order in the object doesn't matter.

checks.question: const { rank, name } = { name: "Bram", rank: 3 }; — what does name equal, even though rank was written first?

feedback.correct: Correct — object destructuring matches by property name, not by the order you list them, so name still gets "Bram".
feedback.incorrect: Object destructuring doesn't care about order — it matches each variable to the property with the same name.

assignment.title: Unpack the Crate
assignment.brief: Write describeItem(item) that destructures item's name and price properties, and returns a string in the form 'Name costs $price'.
requirements: Use object destructuring to pull out name and price in one line.

hints: const { name, price } = item; pulls both values out in one line.
Use a template literal to build the sentence: `${name} costs $${price}`.
Return the built string — don't log it inside the function.
The result for a Hammer priced at 12 should read exactly: Hammer costs $12
